# The Kubestronaut path and what it really costs

> Kubestronaut means holding five CNCF certifications at once: KCNA, KCSA, CKA, CKAD, and CKS. Here's the real cost breakdown, a realistic study timeline, and who it's actually for.

Published: 2026-08-22 · Updated: 2026-08-22 · Tags: kubernetes, certification
Canonical: https://rushabhshah.dev/blog/kubestronaut-path-cost/

Kubestronaut is CNCF's recognition for holding five certifications at the same time: KCNA, KCSA, CKA, CKAD, and CKS. It's not a single exam, it's a status you earn by completing all five and keeping them active simultaneously. People ask me about it a lot at meetups, usually starting with "is it actually worth the money," so let's do the real math instead of just quoting a percentage off.

## What's actually in the bundle

- **KCNA:** Kubernetes and Cloud Native Associate. Multiple choice, no prerequisite, the vocabulary on-ramp.
- **KCSA:** Kubernetes and Cloud Native Security Associate. Also multiple choice, no prerequisite, security concepts instead of general architecture.
- **CKA:** Certified Kubernetes Administrator. Performance-based, live terminal, the cluster-operations cert.
- **CKAD:** Certified Kubernetes Application Developer. Performance-based, the application-layer cert.
- **CKS:** Certified Kubernetes Security Specialist. Performance-based, and the one exam here that requires an active CKA before you can even schedule it.

Two multiple-choice exams to build vocabulary, three hands-on exams to prove you can actually do the job across administration, development, and security.

## The real cost breakdown

Buying each exam individually at list price: $250 + $250 + $445 + $445 + $445 = $1,835. Buying the official Kubestronaut bundle instead brings that down to $1,645, since the bundle itself is already discounted against buying five exams separately. With `RUSHABH30` on top of the bundle price, it drops to roughly $1,151, a saving of about $494 off the bundle price, or close to $684 off what five individual exam purchases would cost.

That's the actual arithmetic, not a marketing percentage. On a purchase this size, 30% off is a meaningfully bigger dollar amount than 30% off any single exam, which is exactly why buying the bundle and applying a discount code to it is the efficient move if you already know you're doing all five.

## A realistic study timeline

I won't pretend there's one true number here, everyone's starting point is different, but here's a reasonable pace if you're consistent and already working with Kubernetes day to day:

- **KCNA and KCSA:** These are pure study, no lab time required. Two to four weeks each if you're working through the material seriously, less if you already have hands-on Kubernetes exposure.
- **CKA:** This is where the pace slows down, because performance-based exams reward muscle memory, not just reading. Budget six to eight weeks of real terminal practice on top of whatever Kubernetes experience you're bringing in.
- **CKAD:** If you've already done CKA, CKAD moves faster since a lot of the terminal fluency transfers. Four to six weeks is realistic.
- **CKS:** Plan this last, since it needs an active CKA. Give it its own six-to-eight-week block focused specifically on hardening, Falco, and supply-chain security rather than general cluster admin, which you've already proven.

Add it up and a realistic full Kubestronaut timeline, done seriously alongside a full-time job, lands somewhere around six to nine months. People who clear it faster are usually already deep in Kubernetes operationally before they start; people who take longer usually aren't studying consistently, which is normal and fine as long as none of your five certifications lapse before you finish the set.

## Is it worth it, and for whom

If you're already administering, developing for, and thinking about securing Kubernetes clusters as part of your actual job, Kubestronaut is a genuinely efficient way to formalize that breadth, and CNCF's public recognition (the badge, the community visibility) is a real, if soft, career signal. If you only need one specific skill validated, chasing all five for the title isn't the efficient path, just get the one cert that matches your actual role from the [CKA vs CKAD vs CKS breakdown](/blog/cka-vs-ckad-vs-cks/).

If five certifications sounds like the floor rather than the ceiling, CNCF also recognizes [Golden Kubestronaut](/linux-foundation-coupon/golden-kubestronaut/) for all sixteen current CNCF and Linux Foundation Kubernetes-ecosystem certifications, and it's an actively growing recognition, not a dormant legacy badge.

`RUSHABH30` takes 30% off the [Kubestronaut bundle](/linux-foundation-coupon/kubestronaut/) or any of the five exams individually. I'm an official Linux Foundation Education affiliate partner, so it costs you nothing extra to use it.

$ five certs, one deadline: don't let the first one expire before you sit the fifth

# Prometheus PCA and OpenTelemetry OTCA, reviewed

> Two multiple-choice, $250 CNCF associate exams for observability: Prometheus PCA leans on PromQL, OTCA leans on the OpenTelemetry API and SDK. Here's an honest read on both, and which to take first.

Published: 2026-08-30 · Updated: 2026-08-30 · Tags: kubernetes, certification
Canonical: https://rushabhshah.dev/blog/pca-otca-review/

Observability is most of my day job, Prometheus, Grafana, Loki, Tempo, and OpenTelemetry, so I get asked a lot about the two CNCF associate exams that cover this space: PCA (Prometheus Certified Associate) and OTCA (OpenTelemetry Certified Associate). Both are $250, both are 90-minute multiple choice, no live terminal for either, and both carry the CNCF official content badge. Here's an honest read on each.

## Prometheus Certified Associate, reviewed

PCA covers observability concepts, Prometheus fundamentals, PromQL, instrumentation and exporters, and alerting and dashboarding. The thing worth knowing going in: PromQL is the largest single domain on the exam, bigger than Prometheus fundamentals itself. That's a deliberate signal about what this credential actually certifies.

Being able to install Prometheus and point Grafana at it is not the same skill as being able to write a PromQL query from scratch to answer a real question about your metrics, and PCA is built to test the second one specifically. If your PromQL is mostly copy-pasted from dashboards you didn't write, that's exactly the gap this exam will find.

Linux Foundation designed it with a specific candidate in mind: people who already hold something like KCNA, CKA, or CKAD, or have a cloud engineering background. If that's you, the Kubernetes context makes the instrumentation and exporters domain click much faster than coming in cold.

## OpenTelemetry Certified Associate, reviewed

OTCA covers observability fundamentals, the OpenTelemetry API and SDK, the OpenTelemetry Collector, and maintaining and debugging observability pipelines. Here the weighting story is even more lopsided: the API and SDK domain alone makes up close to half the exam, well ahead of the Collector domain.

That tells you what OTCA actually validates: real instrumentation knowledge, not just the ability to write a Collector config. If your OpenTelemetry experience so far is "I deployed the Collector someone else configured," this exam is going to test territory you haven't actually touched yet. Exam-takers consistently report the Collector questions use realistic, practical config examples rather than abstract theory, so hands-on time with actual configuration stanzas matters more than reading the spec.

## Which to take first, and why

If your day-to-day already leans on metrics and dashboards, PCA is the natural first move: it validates knowledge you likely already have a head start on, and passing it builds confidence before you tackle OTCA's heavier SDK content. If you're doing greenfield instrumentation work, wiring traces and logs into a new service from scratch, OTCA maps more directly to what you're already doing day to day, and PCA becomes the complementary second exam once you've got metrics backend knowledge to pair with it.

Either order works. They're genuinely complementary rather than sequential: Prometheus handles metrics, OpenTelemetry adds traces and logs to the same picture, and most observability work eventually touches both.

`RUSHABH30` takes 30% off either exam, dropping each from $250 to about $175.

$ get [PCA for ~$175 →](/linux-foundation-coupon/pca/) or [OTCA for ~$175 →](/linux-foundation-coupon/otca/) with RUSHABH30. I'm an official Linux Foundation Education affiliate partner, so the code costs you nothing extra.

# Certification Discount Codes That Actually Work

Updated September 2026 · Two official partner codes, one page

RUSHABH30

RUSHABH_20

I hold two training partnerships, and they cover completely different catalogs on completely different checkouts. That trips people up, so this page exists to answer one question: which code do you need? Once you know, the linked page has the pricing, the exam formats, and the prep advice.

## Which code do you need?

| If you're buying | Use | You save | Where |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Any Linux Foundation or CNCF certification, course or bundle: CKA, CKAD, CKS, KCNA, KCSA, LFCS, LFCA, PCA, OTCA, ICA, CCA, CGOA, CAPA, Kubestronaut | `RUSHABH30` | 30% | training.linuxfoundation.org |
| A FinOps Foundation certification: Practitioner, Engineer, FOCUS Analyst, AI Value, Technology Value | `RUSHABH_20` | 20% | learn.finops.org |

They are not interchangeable. Each checkout rejects the other's code, which is the single most common thing people email me about.

## Linux Foundation & CNCF: 30% off with RUSHABH30

This is the big catalog: every Kubernetes certification, the CNCF associate exams, LFCS and LFCA, the self-paced courses, and the Kubestronaut and Golden Kubestronaut bundles. The code is evergreen with no expiry, and it works on course + exam bundles as well as bare exams, which is usually the better buy. The cheapest way in is KCNA at about $175.

[Full pricing across the catalog, per-exam guides and the sale archive →](https://rushabhshah.dev/linux-foundation-coupon/)

## FinOps Foundation: 20% off with RUSHABH_20

A separate programme covering five self-paced FinOps certifications. Worth knowing up front: this code covers those five specifically and not FinOps Certified Professional, the multi-certification bundles, exam-only purchases, or corporate subscriptions. The cheapest is the FinOps Certified FOCUS Analyst at about $320.

[All five certifications, what the code excludes, and which to take first →](https://rushabhshah.dev/finops-coupon/)

## Not sure which certification, never mind which code?

The short version of advice I give at meetups:

- **You run Kubernetes in production.** [CKA](https://rushabhshah.dev/linux-foundation-coupon/cka/). It's the one hiring managers actually check for, and it's a live-terminal exam so it proves you can do the job rather than describe it.
- **You ship apps onto Kubernetes but don't run the cluster.** [CKAD](https://rushabhshah.dev/linux-foundation-coupon/ckad/).
- **You're new to cloud native.** [KCNA](https://rushabhshah.dev/linux-foundation-coupon/kcna/) for the vocabulary, or [LFCA](https://rushabhshah.dev/linux-foundation-coupon/lfca/) if you're starting further back than that.
- **Your job is cloud cost.** [FinOps Certified Practitioner](https://rushabhshah.dev/finops-coupon/practitioner/), which is the one that gives you and your finance team a shared language.
- **You build cost data pipelines.** [FinOps Certified FOCUS Analyst](https://rushabhshah.dev/finops-coupon/focus-analyst/), the cheapest entry point of the five.

## When a sale beats both codes

## Why it's worth it

AI spend broke most of the assumptions FinOps practices were built on. Token-based pricing has no instance to rightsize, GPU capacity is committed to rather than autoscaled, and a single team can move the monthly bill by an order of magnitude in a week. This is the newest of the five certifications and the one where existing cloud cost instincts transfer least well, which is exactly why it is worth doing deliberately rather than improvising.

## Prep tips

- Go in with your own AI bill in front of you, split into inference, training, and the storage and egress around them, because the allocation material only lands once you can see how blurred those lines are in practice.
- The three levels build on each other, moving from visibility to optimization to forecasting and governance, so resist skipping ahead to the optimization content.
- Treat the forecasting section as the important one. AI budgets fail on estimation far more often than on inefficiency.

**How is FinOps for AI different from regular cloud FinOps?**

The levers change. There is no instance to rightsize on token-priced inference, GPU capacity is committed to rather than scaled on demand, and cost per unit of business value is much harder to attribute. The framework still applies; the specific optimization and allocation techniques do not transfer directly.

**Is this certification worth it if we only use hosted APIs?**

Yes, arguably more so. API-billed AI spend is the easiest kind to lose track of, because it needs no provisioning and shows up as one line on a bill that nobody owns.

## Who this is for

Anyone who generates, ingests, or analyses billing and usage data: data engineers, analysts, platform engineers building cost pipelines, and vendors producing FOCUS-conformant exports.

## What it covers

- What the FOCUS specification is and the problem it solves
- Column definitions, attributes, and metadata
- Reading, validating, and interpreting FOCUS datasets
- Working with billing data consistently across providers
- Best practice for FOCUS-aligned analysis

## Why it's worth it

FOCUS is the most quietly useful thing to come out of the FinOps Foundation. Every provider invented its own billing schema, so multi-cloud cost analysis has always started with weeks of bespoke normalisation before anyone can answer a simple question. FOCUS is the vendor-neutral format that deletes that step. This is also the cheapest of the five offerings and the most directly technical, which makes it the easiest one to justify if you build the pipelines rather than read the dashboards.

## Prep tips

- Pull a real FOCUS export from a provider you use and keep it open while you work through the column definitions, because the specification makes far more sense against actual rows than in the abstract.
- Pay close attention to where costs can be double counted or misattributed when you join datasets, since that is exactly the failure mode the specification exists to prevent.
- The free Introduction to FOCUS course on the same platform is a good half-hour orientation before you start the paid one, and it costs nothing.

## Frequently asked questions

**What is FOCUS?**

FOCUS is the FinOps Open Cost and Usage Specification, an open, vendor-neutral schema for cloud billing and usage data. It lets cost data from different providers be read with one set of column definitions instead of a bespoke parser per vendor.

**How much is the FinOps Certified FOCUS Analyst with a discount code?**

It lists at $400, the cheapest of the five offerings this code covers. With RUSHABH_20 it comes to about $320.

**Do I need to know SQL for the FOCUS Analyst certification?**

Not formally. The FinOps Foundation suggests familiarity with basic data analysis and some awareness of how providers produce billing data. Experience querying datasets helps but is not required.

**Should I take FOCP or FOCUS Analyst first?**

If you work on cost data pipelines, FOCUS Analyst stands on its own and you can start there. If you need the wider practice context first, take Practitioner and add FOCUS Analyst after.

**Is there a free way to learn FOCUS?**

Yes. The FinOps Foundation publishes a free Introduction to FOCUS course. It will not certify you, but it is a genuine introduction and worth doing before you pay for the full certification.

## What the code does not cover

Worth stating plainly, because most coupon pages imply a code works on everything. The FinOps Foundation approved five offerings for this code. These are **not** included:

- FinOps Certified Professional, the advanced certification
- The multi-certification bundles, such as Practitioner + FOCUS Analyst or the Full Catalog plan
- FinOps for Containers
- Exam-only and recertification purchases
- Corporate training subscriptions

If you're weighing a bundle against buying two certifications separately with the code, do the arithmetic both ways. Sometimes the bundle still wins, and I'd rather you saved the money than used my code.

## Which FinOps certification should you take first?

**Almost everyone should start with the [FinOps Certified Practitioner](https://rushabhshah.dev/finops-coupon/practitioner/).** It is the one job descriptions name, and more usefully it is the one that gives you and your finance team a shared vocabulary. The other four assume you already have it.

Two reasonable exceptions:

- If you build and run the infrastructure and want cost folded into engineering decisions rather than reported after the fact, [FinOps Certified Engineer](https://rushabhshah.dev/finops-coupon/engineer/) is the better fit and reads as the more relevant credential on an engineering CV.
- If your actual job is billing data pipelines and cost reporting, [FinOps Certified FOCUS Analyst](https://rushabhshah.dev/finops-coupon/focus-analyst/) stands on its own, and at $400 it is the cheapest way into the catalog.

[AI Value](https://rushabhshah.dev/finops-coupon/ai-value/) and [Technology Value](https://rushabhshah.dev/finops-coupon/technology-value/) are both extensions of an existing practice rather than entry points. Take them when the question they answer is one your leadership is actually asking: AI Value when AI spend has become material and nobody can explain it, Technology Value when the remit has grown past public cloud into SaaS, data centres, and data platforms.

## Frequently asked questions

**Is RUSHABH_20 legit?**

Yes. It's a promo code issued to me directly by the FinOps Foundation as a promotional partner. It isn't scraped or recycled from a coupon aggregator, and it's honoured at checkout on learn.finops.org.

**Which FinOps offerings does it work on?**

Five: FinOps Certified Practitioner, FinOps Certified Engineer, FinOps Certified FOCUS Analyst, FinOps Certified: AI Value, and FinOps Certified: Technology Value, each as the Self-Paced Course + Certification Exam offering. Not FinOps Certified Professional, the bundles, FinOps for Containers, exam-only or recertification purchases, or corporate subscriptions.

**How much does FinOps certification cost with the code?**

The four $500 offerings come to about $400 each, and the FOCUS Analyst certification goes from $400 to about $320. That's 20% off, so $80 to $100 saved per certification.

**Does it stack with other discounts?**

No. Promo codes on learn.finops.org don't combine. Use whichever single discount is larger.

**Does the code expire?**

No end date was set when it was issued. This page rebuilds daily, so if the code ever stops working it gets corrected here rather than left up as a dead coupon.

**Does RUSHABH30 work on these FinOps certifications?**

Not on learn.finops.org, which is where these five certifications are sold. They're two separate partner programmes on two separate checkouts: RUSHABH30 applies at training.linuxfoundation.org and RUSHABH_20 applies at learn.finops.org. Use [RUSHABH30](https://rushabhshah.dev/linux-foundation-coupon/) for CKA, CKAD, CKS, KCNA and the rest of the CNCF catalog, and RUSHABH_20 here.

**Is FinOps certification worth it at all?**

It depends what you want from it. It won't teach an experienced engineer new ways to cut a bill. What it gives you is a framework and a shared language for defending cost decisions to finance and leadership, which is usually the harder half of the work, plus a credential that's increasingly named in cloud cost job descriptions.

*List price read from the FinOps Foundation's own catalog in September 2026. They set the prices and can revise them, so check [the product page](https://learn.finops.org/path/finops-certified-practitioner-self-paced) for the current number before you buy.*

## Who this is for

Anyone who touches a cloud bill: finance, engineering, procurement, and product people who need one shared language for cost, usage, and value. It is the default first FinOps certification.

## What it covers

- What FinOps is, and the FinOps Framework
- FinOps teams, culture, personas, and motivations
- FinOps domains and capabilities
- Anatomy of the cloud bill, and the data in the path
- The Inform, Optimize, and Operate phases
- Adopting and maturing a FinOps practice

## Why it's worth it

FOCP is the one FinOps credential most job descriptions actually name. The real value is not the badge, it is the vocabulary: once your finance team and your platform team both say "allocation", "unit economics" and "showback" to mean the same thing, cost conversations stop being arguments about whose number is right. Everything else in the FinOps catalog assumes you already have this.

## Prep tips

- Bring a real bill. Open your own AWS, Azure, or GCP cost console next to the course and map each concept onto spend you actually recognise, because the exam rewards understanding the shape of a bill rather than memorising definitions.
- The Inform, Optimize, Operate loop is the spine of the whole framework and the thing most questions hang off, so get comfortable placing any given activity into the right phase.
- Do not skip the personas material even though it feels soft next to the billing content. A meaningful slice of the exam is about who cares about which metric and why.

## Frequently asked questions

**Is the FinOps Certified Practitioner exam hands-on?**

No. It is a multiple-choice exam you complete online at your own pace, with no live console or terminal work. Enrolment includes the exam alongside the course.

**How much is the FinOps Certified Practitioner with a discount code?**

The self-paced course plus certification exam lists at $500. With RUSHABH_20 it comes to about $400, saving roughly $100.

**Do I need a prerequisite for FOCP?**

No formal prerequisite. The FinOps Foundation recommends a general understanding of infrastructure, usage-based pricing, and familiarity with at least one major cloud provider.

**How long does the FinOps Practitioner certification last?**

The certification is valid for 24 months, and your enrolment includes 12 months of access to the course materials.

**Does RUSHABH_20 work on the exam-only option?**

No. The code covers the Self-Paced Course + Certification Exam offering. The cheaper exam-only SKU is not one of the five offerings the FinOps Foundation approved for this code.

**Is FOCP worth it if I already do cloud cost work?**

If you already cut spend for a living, the framework will not teach you new levers. What it gives you is the shared structure and language to defend those decisions to finance and leadership, which is usually the harder half of the job.

## Quick facts

| **Offering** | Self-Paced Course + Certification Exam |
| --- | --- |
| **Format** | Multiple choice, online, self-directed |

*List price read from the FinOps Foundation's own catalog in September 2026. They set the prices and can revise them, so check [the product page](https://learn.finops.org/path/technology-value) for the current number before you buy.*

## Who this is for

Established practitioners whose remit has grown past public cloud into data centres, SaaS, and data platforms, and who need the framework to stretch that far.

## What it covers

- Defining and managing FinOps Scopes
- Applying the FinOps Framework beyond public cloud
- Public cloud, data centre, SaaS, and data cloud platforms as distinct categories
- How capabilities, personas, and optimization levers differ per category
- Connecting technology spend to business strategy and outcomes
- Driving executive alignment on technology investment

## Why it's worth it

Most FinOps practices hit the same wall: the cloud bill gets well managed, and then someone points out that SaaS licences, the remaining data centre, and the data platform together cost more than the cloud does. This is the certification for widening the practice without abandoning the framework, and Scopes are the piece that makes that tractable rather than infinite.

## Prep tips

- List every technology cost category your organisation actually carries before you start, including the ones nobody currently owns, and use that list as the worked example throughout.
- Scopes are the load-bearing concept in this course. Getting precise about what your practice does and does not cover is most of the value on offer.
- Each category has genuinely different cost structures and data models, so resist mapping cloud habits onto SaaS or data centre spend.

## How to use the code

- Open the [FinOps Certified: Technology Value page](https://learn.finops.org/path/technology-value) on learn.finops.org and choose the Self-Paced Course + Certification Exam option.
- Enter `RUSHABH_20` in the promo code field and apply it before paying.
- Check the total actually dropped by 20%. If it didn't, you've probably selected an exam-only, bundle, or subscription SKU, which this code doesn't cover.

RUSHABH_20

[Apply it at checkout →](https://learn.finops.org/path/technology-value)

## Frequently asked questions

**What are FinOps Scopes?**

Scopes are how a FinOps practice declares what it covers. They set the boundary and the shared expectations around which technology categories, such as public cloud, SaaS, or data centre, the practice actually operates in.

**How much is FinOps Certified: Technology Value with a discount code?**

The self-paced course plus certification exam lists at $500. With RUSHABH_20 it comes to about $400.

**Do I need to be a FinOps Practitioner first?**

Not formally, but the FinOps Foundation recommends completing FinOps Certified Practitioner or FinOps Certified Engineer beforehand, since the course builds directly on framework knowledge.

**Is this useful if we are cloud only?**

Less so today, more so later. If you have no data centre and minimal SaaS, start elsewhere. The moment someone asks you to account for SaaS licences or a data platform, this is the certification that has already thought about it.

**How does this compare to FinOps Certified: AI Value?**

They are siblings, both extending an existing practice into new territory. AI Value goes deep on one fast-moving category; Technology Value goes wide across the whole portfolio. Pick by whichever question your leadership is actually asking.

# CAPA Discount Code: 30% Off with RUSHABH30

Updated September 2026 · Certified Argo Project Associate

RUSHABH30

[Get CAPA for ~$175 →](https://www.awin1.com/cread.php?awinmid=85919&awinaffid=2950265&ued=https%3A%2F%2Ftraining.linuxfoundation.org%2Fcertification%2Fcertified-argo-project-associate-capa%2F)

Put `RUSHABH30` in the coupon field at checkout on [training.linuxfoundation.org](https://www.awin1.com/cread.php?awinmid=85919&awinaffid=2950265&ued=https%3A%2F%2Ftraining.linuxfoundation.org%2Fcertification%2Fcertified-argo-project-associate-capa%2F) and the Certified Argo Project Associate (CAPA) exam drops from $250 to about $175, a saving of roughly $75. It's an evergreen partner code with no expiry, issued directly to me through the official Linux Foundation Education affiliate program.

## Quick facts

| **Format** | Multiple choice, online proctored |
| --- | --- |
| **Duration** | 90 minutes |
| **List price** | $250 |
| **With RUSHABH30** | ~$175 |
| **Prerequisite** | None |

## Who this is for

Teams running any part of the Argo suite, particularly Argo CD for delivery or Workflows for batch work.

## What it covers

- Argo Workflows (36%)
- Argo CD (34%)
- Argo Rollouts (18%)
- Argo Events (12%)

*Domain names above reflect the current official curriculum's topic areas; exact weightings are set by the Linux Foundation/CNCF and revised periodically, so check their published curriculum for the current breakdown.*

## Why it's worth it

Worth checking the weighting before you buy, because it surprises people: Workflows is the single largest domain at 36%, slightly ahead of Argo CD. If you came for GitOps and have never run a Workflow, that is over a third of the exam on a tool you do not use. Genuinely useful if your shop runs the suite; a poor choice if you only run Argo CD.

## Prep tips

- Do not assume this is an Argo CD exam. Workflows and Argo CD are 70% between them and Workflows is the bigger half, so budget your preparation accordingly.
- Argo Rollouts at 18% means progressive delivery is worth real study: analysis templates, AnalysisRun, and how a canary actually decides to proceed.
- Argo Events is only 12% but it is the piece most people have never touched. It is cheap marks if you spend an evening on it.

## How to use the code

## What it covers

- Architecture (20%)

- Service mesh (16%)

- Installation and configuration (10%)
- Cluster mesh (10%)
- eBPF (10%)
- BGP and external networking (6%)

*Domain names above reflect the current official curriculum's topic areas; exact weightings are set by the Linux Foundation/CNCF and revised periodically, so check their published curriculum for the current breakdown.*

## Why it's worth it

The most evenly spread exam in the catalogue: eight domains, none above 20%, so there is nowhere to hide. It is also the only certification here that makes you learn eBPF properly, which is increasingly the answer to "how is this doing networking without iptables". Worth it if you run Cilium, and defensible as a learning structure even if you do not.

## Prep tips

- Install Cilium on a throwaway cluster and turn Hubble on. Network observability and eBPF are 20% combined, and both make far more sense once you have watched flows rather than read about them.
- Network policy is 18% and the Cilium model differs from stock Kubernetes NetworkPolicy. Learn both and learn where they diverge.
- Do not skip cluster mesh and BGP because they are only 16% together. With eight domains, dropping two entirely is most of your margin.

List price is $250. With RUSHABH30 it drops to about $175, a saving of roughly $75.

**Do I need to know eBPF first?**

No, and the exam only weights eBPF at 10%. But Cilium is built on it, so the parts that look like magic stop looking that way once you understand roughly what the kernel is doing.

**Is CCA performance-based?**

No, it is multiple choice. Istio's ICA is the performance-based one of the two mesh-adjacent associate exams, which is worth knowing if you want the stronger signal.

## Who this is for

Anyone doing continuous delivery who wants the principles rather than one vendor's implementation of them.

## What it covers

- GitOps terminology (20%)
- GitOps principles (30%)
- Related practices (16%)
- GitOps patterns (20%)
- Tooling (14%)

*Domain names above reflect the current official curriculum's topic areas; exact weightings are set by the Linux Foundation/CNCF and revised periodically, so check their published curriculum for the current breakdown.*

## Why it's worth it

The tool-agnostic one, and the only exam here where tooling is the smallest domain at 14%. That is the point: it certifies that you understand declarative desired state, continuous reconciliation and drift, rather than which buttons a particular controller has. If you have been doing GitOps by copying someone else's Argo config, this is the exam that makes you understand why it works.

## Prep tips

- Principles and patterns are half the exam. Be able to explain state drift, reconciliation and rollback in your own words before you touch a practice test.
- The terminology domain is 20% and it is precise. The GitOps working group has written definitions, and the exam uses them rather than the loose industry usage.
- Do not over-prepare tooling. It is 14%, and candidates routinely spend most of their time there because it is the comfortable part.

## How to use the code

## Frequently asked questions

**What is the CGOA certification?**

The Certified GitOps Associate, a 90-minute multiple-choice exam on GitOps terminology, principles, patterns and related practices. Deliberately tool-agnostic.

**How much is the CGOA with a discount code?**

List price is $250. With RUSHABH30 it drops to about $175, a saving of roughly $75.

**Do I need to know Argo or Flux?**

Not specifically. Tooling is the smallest domain at 14%, and the exam is written to be implementation-neutral. Experience with either helps, but neither is assumed.

**Is CGOA worth it if I already do GitOps daily?**

Honestly, less than you would hope. It certifies understanding rather than skill, so its value is mostly to people formalising knowledge or needing the credential on paper. If you already run reconciling delivery and nobody is asking you to prove it, spend the money elsewhere.

## Who this is for

Ops, platform engineering, and SRE roles who run Kubernetes clusters day to day.

## What it covers

- Cluster architecture, installation, and configuration
- Workloads and scheduling
- Services and networking
- Storage
- Troubleshooting cluster and application issues

*Domain names above reflect the current official curriculum's topic areas; exact weightings are set by the Linux Foundation/CNCF and revised periodically, so check their published curriculum for the current breakdown.*

## Why it's worth it

The CKA is the credential hiring managers actually check for when a role involves running Kubernetes in production, not just deploying to it. It's a live-terminal, performance-based exam. You fix real broken clusters against the clock, not multiple-choice questions. So it certifies you can actually do the job, not just describe it.

## Prep tips

- Practice in a real terminal daily in the weeks before. This exam is a speed test as much as a knowledge test, and muscle memory for kubectl and vim matters more than reading about concepts.
- Get comfortable with the allowed documentation (kubernetes.io) during practice, since you're allowed to reference it in the real exam. Know where to find things fast rather than memorizing everything.
- Troubleshooting is the single biggest domain, so spend disproportionate practice time deliberately breaking and fixing clusters, not just deploying happy-path workloads.

## Frequently asked questions

**Is the CKA exam multiple-choice?**

No. It's 100% performance-based: you're given a live terminal and a set of real Kubernetes clusters, and you complete hands-on tasks against the clock. There's no multiple-choice section.

**Do I need any prerequisite certification for the CKA?**

No. The CKA has no certification prerequisite, though the Linux Foundation recommends some hands-on Kubernetes experience first.

**How much is the CKA with a discount code?**

List price is $445. With RUSHABH30 it drops to about $311, a saving of roughly $134.

**Does RUSHABH30 work on the CKA course + exam bundle?**

Yes. The 30% applies whether you buy the exam alone or bundled with the official prep course, and the bundle is usually the better value since it's already discounted before the code applies.

**What's actually included in the $445, not just the exam attempt?**

One free retake if you don't pass the first time, two exam simulator attempts (36 hours of access each, from activation), and a 12-month window to schedule and sit the exam after purchase. Most coupon pages only mention the price and skip this.

**What should I do after passing the CKA?**

The natural next steps are the CKAD if you also ship applications to Kubernetes, or the CKS if you want the strongest Kubernetes security signal on your CV. CKS requires an active CKA to sit.

## Why it's worth it

They need to know pods, deployments, config, probes, and how to debug their own workloads fast. It's the same performance-based format as the CKA, just scoped to the application layer instead of the platform layer.

## Prep tips

- Focus practice time on the manifest types you'll actually write day to day (Deployments, ConfigMaps, Secrets, and probes), since the exam rewards speed writing and editing YAML under time pressure.
- Practice debugging a broken Pod from logs and describe output alone; a meaningful slice of the exam is "this deployment is failing, find out why."
- Like the CKA, you can reference kubernetes.io during the exam. Practice navigating to the exact page you need instead of trying to memorize every flag.

## Frequently asked questions

**Is the CKAD easier than the CKA?**

It's narrower, not necessarily easier. CKAD skips cluster-administration topics but goes deep on the application layer (config, probes, multi-container pod patterns) that the CKA only touches lightly.

**Do I need the CKA before taking the CKAD?**

No. CKAD has no certification prerequisite and is commonly taken by developers who never plan to sit the CKA at all.

**How much is the CKAD with a discount code?**

List price is $445. With RUSHABH30 it drops to about $311.

**Is the CKAD hands-on or multiple-choice?**

Hands-on. Like the CKA, it's a live-terminal, performance-based exam against real clusters, with no multiple-choice questions.

**Does RUSHABH30 work on the CKAD course + exam bundle?**

Yes, on the exam alone or bundled with the official prep course.

People moving toward platform engineering who want the vocabulary and the shape of the discipline before committing to the performance-based exam.

## What it covers

- Platform engineering core fundamentals (36%)

- Continuous delivery and platform engineering (16%)
- Platform APIs and provisioning infrastructure (12%)
- Internal developer platforms and developer experience (8%)
- Measuring your platform (8%)

*Domain names above reflect the current official curriculum's topic areas; exact weightings are set by the Linux Foundation/CNCF and revised periodically, so check their published curriculum for the current breakdown.*

## Why it's worth it

Platform engineering suffers from being a job title before it was a defined discipline, and this exam is the Linux Foundation writing down what it thinks the discipline is. Over a third of it is core fundamentals, which is unusually top-heavy and tells you it is aimed at people who have not done the job yet. Useful as an orientation and as the step below CNPE.

## Prep tips

- Pay attention to the measurement domain. It is only 8% but it is the part most practitioners have never thought about, and the one that separates a platform from a pile of tooling.
- You do not need to have built an internal developer platform, but you should have used one and be able to say what made it good or bad.
- Multiple choice and 120 minutes, so it is a recall exam. Read the curriculum and map each item to something you have seen rather than practising in a terminal.

List price is $250. With RUSHABH30 it drops to about $175, a saving of roughly $75.

**CNPA or CNPE, which should I take?**

CNPA if you are moving into platform work and want the map. CNPE if you already do it and want a credential that proves you can build. CNPA is the cheaper, multiple-choice orientation; CNPE is performance-based at $445.

None formally. In practice you will struggle without hands-on Kubernetes experience, since almost every domain assumes a cluster underneath.

It's an evergreen partner code with no expiry, issued directly to me through the official Linux Foundation Education affiliate program.

## Quick facts

| **Format** | Performance-based (live terminal) |
| --- | --- |
| **Duration** | 2 hours |
| **List price** | $445 |
| **With RUSHABH30** | ~$311 |
| **Prerequisite** | None |

## Who this is for

Engineers who build the internal platform other teams ship on, rather than operating a cluster directly.

## What it covers

- Platform architecture and infrastructure (15%)
- GitOps and continuous delivery (25%)
- Platform APIs and self-service capabilities (25%)
- Observability and operations (20%)
- Security and policy enforcement (15%)

*Domain names above reflect the current official curriculum's topic areas; exact weightings are set by the Linux Foundation/CNCF and revised periodically, so check their published curriculum for the current breakdown.*

## Why it's worth it

The most senior exam in the cloud native catalogue and the only one that tests design judgement rather than operation. It is performance-based at the same price as the CKA, and the weighting tells you what it cares about: half the exam is delivery and self-service APIs, which is the part of platform engineering people usually learn by getting it wrong in production first. Do not treat it as a first certification. It assumes everything the CKA covers.

## Prep tips

- Build a real self-service path end to end before sitting it, even a small one. The exam rewards having designed an interface other engineers consume, and that is hard to fake from reading.
- GitOps and continuous delivery is 25% on its own. If your delivery experience is pipeline scripts rather than a reconciling controller, close that gap first.
- It is a live terminal like the CKA, so the same advice applies: practise against the clock, and know where the documentation lives rather than memorising flags.

## How to use the code

- Add the CNPE exam to your cart on [training.linuxfoundation.org](https://www.awin1.com/cread.php?awinmid=85919&awinaffid=2950265&ued=https%3A%2F%2Ftraining.linuxfoundation.org%2Fcertification%2Fcertified-cloud-native-platform-engineer-cnpe%2F).
- Enter `RUSHABH30` in the coupon field at checkout.
- The total drops 30%. RUSHABH30 works on the exam with one free retake, within a 12-month eligibility window.

[Apply it at checkout →](https://www.awin1.com/cread.php?awinmid=85919&awinaffid=2950265&ued=https%3A%2F%2Ftraining.linuxfoundation.org%2Fcertification%2Fcertified-cloud-native-platform-engineer-cnpe%2F)

## Frequently asked questions

**What is the CNPE certification?**

The Certified Cloud Native Platform Engineer, a performance-based Linux Foundation exam covering platform architecture, GitOps delivery, self-service APIs, observability and policy enforcement. Two hours in a live terminal.

**How much is the CNPE with a discount code?**

List price is $445. With RUSHABH30 it drops to about $311, a saving of roughly $134.

**Is the CNPE harder than the CKA?**

Different rather than harder. The CKA tests whether you can operate a cluster; the CNPE tests whether you can design something other engineers build on top of. It assumes CKA-level knowledge as a starting point.

**Should this be my first certification?**

No. It is aimed at people already doing platform work. If you are new to Kubernetes, the CKA is the better purchase and the natural prerequisite in practice, even though it is not a formal one.

**What is the difference between CNPE and CNPA?**

CNPA is the associate-level, multiple-choice version covering the same territory at a recall level. CNPE is performance-based and costs more because it asks you to actually build. CNPA is the sensible stepping stone.

*Domain names above reflect the current official curriculum's topic areas; exact weightings are set by the Linux Foundation/CNCF and revised periodically, so check their published curriculum for the current breakdown.*

## Why it's worth it

Golden Kubestronaut is CNCF's recognition for holding every one of its certifications at once: sixteen exams, not five. CNCF launched the program in April 2025, and over 100 engineers had already earned the title within five months, so this is an actively growing recognition, not a legacy badge nobody pursues. On a purchase this size, RUSHABH30 produces the single biggest dollar saving it generates on this entire site. More than double the five-exam Kubestronaut bundle, simply because there are more than three times as many exams for the same 30% to apply to.

## Prep tips

- Sequence the sixteen exams deliberately: CKS still needs an active CKA even inside this bigger bundle, so don't buy the exams in a random order.
- Clear the eleven multiple-choice associate exams (KCNA, KCSA, PCA, ICA, CCA, CAPA, CGOA, CBA, OTCA, KCA, CNPA) first to build momentum before the four performance-based, live-terminal exams (CKA, CKAD, CKS, LFCS).
- Linux Foundation's own program page notes new CNCF certifications can be added to the requirement list as they launch. Budget for the list to grow past sixteen, not assume it's fixed forever.

## Frequently asked questions

**What is Golden Kubestronaut?**

CNCF's recognition for holding all 16 current CNCF and Linux Foundation Kubernetes-ecosystem certifications simultaneously: the full catalog, not just the five-exam Kubestronaut track.

**How much does the Golden Kubestronaut bundle cost with a discount code?**

List price is $4229 for all sixteen exams. With RUSHABH30 it drops to about $2960, a saving of roughly $1,269, the largest single saving RUSHABH30 produces on any purchase on this site.

**Do I need the regular Kubestronaut certification before Golden Kubestronaut?**

There's no separate application step. Golden Kubestronaut is earned simply by holding all 16 certifications, which happen to include the same five that make up standard Kubestronaut (KCNA, KCSA, CKA, CKAD, CKS) plus eleven more.

**Is Golden Kubestronaut a real, active program?**

Yes. CNCF launched it in April 2025, and Linux Foundation reported over 100 engineers had achieved it within the first five months. It's actively promoted, not a dormant legacy title.

**Can the certification list change?**

Yes. Linux Foundation's own program page states that as new CNCF certifications launch, they may be added to the Golden Kubestronaut requirements to keep the badge current.

Put `RUSHABH30` in the coupon field at checkout on [training.linuxfoundation.org](https://www.awin1.com/cread.php?awinmid=85919&awinaffid=2950265&ued=https%3A%2F%2Ftraining.linuxfoundation.org%2Fcertification%2Fistio-certified-associate-ica%2F) and the Istio Certified Associate (ICA) exam drops from $250 to about $175, a saving of roughly $75. ## Quick facts

| **Format** | Performance-based (live terminal) |
| --- | --- |
| **Duration** | 2 hours |
| **List price** | $250 |
| **With RUSHABH30** | ~$175 |
| **Prerequisite** | None |

## Who this is for

Engineers running or about to run Istio, who need to prove they can configure traffic and mTLS rather than describe them.

## What it covers

- Installation, upgrade and configuration (20%)
- Traffic management (35%)
- Securing workloads (25%)
- Troubleshooting (20%)

*Domain names above reflect the current official curriculum's topic areas; exact weightings are set by the Linux Foundation/CNCF and revised periodically, so check their published curriculum for the current breakdown.*

## Why it's worth it

One of the few associate-level exams that is performance-based rather than multiple choice, which makes it worth noticeably more than its "associate" label suggests. Traffic management alone is 35%, so it is largely about whether you can express routing, retries and failure injection correctly under time pressure. Only worth taking if you actually run Istio; a mesh certification on top of shaky networking fundamentals is a poor trade.

## Prep tips

- Practise in a real mesh with real traffic. The traffic-management domain is a third of the exam and it is all configuration you either have written before or have not.
- Know the difference between a VirtualService and a DestinationRule cold. Confusing the two is the classic way to lose time.
- Troubleshooting is 20%, so deliberately break your mesh and fix it: misapplied policy, wrong namespace, sidecar not injected.

## How to use the code

- Add the ICA exam to your cart on [training.linuxfoundation.org](https://www.awin1.com/cread.php?awinmid=85919&awinaffid=2950265&ued=https%3A%2F%2Ftraining.linuxfoundation.org%2Fcertification%2Fistio-certified-associate-ica%2F).
- Enter `RUSHABH30` in the coupon field at checkout.
- The total drops 30%. RUSHABH30 works on the exam with one free retake, within a 12-month eligibility window.

RUSHABH30

[Apply it at checkout →](https://www.awin1.com/cread.php?awinmid=85919&awinaffid=2950265&ued=https%3A%2F%2Ftraining.linuxfoundation.org%2Fcertification%2Fistio-certified-associate-ica%2F)

## Frequently asked questions

**Is the ICA multiple choice?**

No. Unusually for an associate-level exam it is performance-based: a live terminal with a real mesh, two hours. That makes it stronger evidence than most associate certifications.

**How much is the ICA with a discount code?**

List price is $250. With RUSHABH30 it drops to about $175, a saving of roughly $75.

**Do I need the CKA before the ICA?**

Not formally, and there is no prerequisite. In practice a service mesh sits on top of Kubernetes networking, so if pods, services and DNS are still hazy, learn those first or the mesh will look like magic.

**ICA or CCA, which is more useful?**

Whichever you actually run. ICA is Istio, CCA is Cilium, and they solve overlapping problems in very different ways. Taking the one your employer does not use is an expensive way to learn a tool you will not touch.

## Which certification is actually worth it?

I get this question at almost every meetup, so here's the advice I actually give, not the brochure version:

- **Completely new to cloud-native?** Start with KCNA. It's multiple-choice, it's the cheap one, and it forces you to learn the landscape's vocabulary before you touch a cluster in anger.
- **Working in ops, SRE, or platform engineering?** Go straight for the CKA. It's a live-terminal exam, not multiple choice, hiring managers respect it, and the prep transfers directly to your day job.
- **A developer who ships to Kubernetes?** CKAD covers pods, deployments, config, probes and debugging. Everything you need, none of the cluster-administration depth you won't use.
- **Already have the CKA?** CKS is the natural next step and one of the strongest security signals you can put on a DevOps CV right now.
- **Shaky on Linux itself?** Do LFCS first. Kubernetes problems are very often just Linux problems wearing a trench coat.

## Don't buy prep until you've used the free stuff

Buy the exam with the discount, sure, but exhaust the free material before paying for prep. I maintain free exam-prep repositories on GitHub ([AWS SAA-C03](https://github.com/Iamrushabhshahh/AWS-Certified-Solutions-Architect-Associate-SAA-C03-Exam-Dump-With-Solution), [Azure AZ-104](https://github.com/Iamrushabhshahh/Microsoft-Azure-Administrator-AZ-104-Exam-Dump-Question-With-Solution)) and write hands-on Kubernetes and observability guides on [my blog](https://rushabhshah.dev/blog/). For CKA/CKAD/CKS specifically: practice in a real terminal daily. Those exams are speed tests as much as knowledge tests, and no amount of video-watching substitutes for muscle memory.

## Quick facts

| **Format** | Multiple choice, online proctored |
| --- | --- |

## Who this is for

Platform and security engineers who enforce cluster policy, or are about to be asked to.

## What it covers

- Fundamentals of Kyverno (18%)
- Installation, configuration and upgrades (18%)
- Kyverno CLI (12%)
- Applying policies (10%)
- Writing policies (32%)
- Policy management (10%)

*Domain names above reflect the current official curriculum's topic areas; exact weightings are set by the Linux Foundation/CNCF and revised periodically, so check their published curriculum for the current breakdown.*

## Why it's worth it

Almost a third of this exam is writing policies, which is the correct emphasis and also the reason it is harder than its beginner label suggests. Kyverno's pitch is policy as Kubernetes resources rather than a separate language, so if you have bounced off Rego and OPA before, this is the friendlier route into admission control.

## Prep tips

- Writing policies is 32%. Write them, repeatedly, against a real cluster. Validate, mutate and generate rules all behave differently and the exam covers all three.
- Learn the CLI properly. It is 12% and it is also how you will test policies without deploying them, which makes the rest of the preparation faster.
- Understand where admission control sits in the request path. Several questions become obvious once you know when a policy actually runs.

## How to use the code

- Add the KCA exam to your cart on [training.linuxfoundation.org](https://www.awin1.com/cread.php?awinmid=85919&awinaffid=2950265&ued=https%3A%2F%2Ftraining.linuxfoundation.org%2Fcertification%2Fkyverno-certified-associate-kca%2F).
- Enter `RUSHABH30` in the coupon field at checkout.
- The total drops 30%. RUSHABH30 works on the exam with one free retake, within a 12-month eligibility window.

RUSHABH30

[Apply it at checkout →](https://www.awin1.com/cread.php?awinmid=85919&awinaffid=2950265&ued=https%3A%2F%2Ftraining.linuxfoundation.org%2Fcertification%2Fkyverno-certified-associate-kca%2F)

## Frequently asked questions

**What is the KCA certification?**

The Kyverno Certified Associate, a 90-minute multiple-choice exam on Kyverno fundamentals, installation, the CLI, and writing, applying and managing policies.

**How much is the KCA with a discount code?**

List price is $250. With RUSHABH30 it drops to about $175, a saving of roughly $75.

**Is KCA a security certification?**

Partly. It covers policy enforcement, which is a security control, but it is narrower than the CKS. If you want a broad Kubernetes security credential, CKS is the one; KCA proves you can enforce policy with a specific tool.

**Kyverno or OPA?**

Kyverno expresses policy as Kubernetes resources, OPA uses Rego, a separate language. Neither is objectively better, but Kyverno has the gentler learning curve for people who already think in YAML manifests. This exam only covers Kyverno.

Updated September 2026 · Model Context Protocol Associate

RUSHABH30

[Get MCPA for ~$175 →](https://www.awin1.com/cread.php?awinmid=85919&awinaffid=2950265&ued=https%3A%2F%2Ftraining.linuxfoundation.org%2Fcertification%2Fmodel-context-protocol-associate-mcpa%2F)

Put `RUSHABH30` in the coupon field at checkout on [training.linuxfoundation.org](https://www.awin1.com/cread.php?awinmid=85919&awinaffid=2950265&ued=https%3A%2F%2Ftraining.linuxfoundation.org%2Fcertification%2Fmodel-context-protocol-associate-mcpa%2F) and the Model Context Protocol Associate (MCPA) exam drops from $250 to about $175, a saving of roughly $75. It's an evergreen partner code with no expiry, issued directly to me through the official Linux Foundation Education affiliate program.

## Quick facts

| **Format** | Online, proctored, multiple-choice |
| --- | --- |
| **Duration** | 90 minutes |
| **List price** | $250 |
| **With RUSHABH30** | ~$175 |
| **Prerequisite** | None |

## Who this is for

Engineers building AI assistants, agents and tool integrations, who need to show they understand how MCP actually wires a model to external tools and data.

## What it covers

- MCP fundamentals: purpose, scope and core concepts (16%)
- Architecture and components: hosts, clients, servers and schemas (14%)
- Interactions and execution: interaction patterns, tool invocation lifecycle, error handling (26%)
- Security and governance: trust boundaries, permissions and consent, auditability (24%)
- Use cases and ecosystem: adoption, operational use cases, portability (20%)

*Domain names above reflect the current official curriculum's topic areas; exact weightings are set by the Linux Foundation/CNCF and revised periodically, so check their published curriculum for the current breakdown.*

## Why it's worth it

MCP went from an Anthropic specification to the way most agent tooling talks to external systems in about a year, and this is the first certification against it. It is worth a look mainly because of what it weights: half the exam is interactions and execution plus security and governance, which is the half people actually get wrong. Writing an MCP server is easy, and reasoning about trust boundaries and consent when a model can invoke your tools is not. It is a beginner-level, multiple-choice exam, so treat it as evidence you have thought about the protocol properly rather than as a senior credential.

## Prep tips

- Build a small MCP server and connect a real client to it before reading anything else. The interaction and tool-invocation lifecycle is 26% of the exam and it makes far more sense once you have watched the messages go back and forth.
- Do not skim the security domain. Trust boundaries, permissions and consent are 24% on their own, and they are the part that a purely hands-on background tends to leave thin.
- Read the specification itself rather than only blog posts about it. It is short, it is the source the exam is written from, and MCP has moved quickly enough that third-party write-ups go stale fast.

## How to use the code

- Add the MCPA exam to your cart on [training.linuxfoundation.org](https://www.awin1.com/cread.php?awinmid=85919&awinaffid=2950265&ued=https%3A%2F%2Ftraining.linuxfoundation.org%2Fcertification%2Fmodel-context-protocol-associate-mcpa%2F).
- Enter `RUSHABH30` in the coupon field at checkout.
- The total drops 30%. RUSHABH30 works on the exam with one free retake included, within a 12-month eligibility window.

[Apply it at checkout →](https://www.awin1.com/cread.php?awinmid=85919&awinaffid=2950265&ued=https%3A%2F%2Ftraining.linuxfoundation.org%2Fcertification%2Fmodel-context-protocol-associate-mcpa%2F)

## Frequently asked questions

**What is the MCPA certification?**

The Model Context Protocol Associate, a Linux Foundation certification covering MCP: how hosts, clients and servers fit together, how tool invocation and error handling work, and the security model around letting a model call your tools. It is an online, proctored, multiple-choice exam of 90 minutes.

**How much is the MCPA with a discount code?**

List price is $250. With RUSHABH30 it drops to about $175, a saving of roughly $75.

**Are there prerequisites for the MCPA?**

No. The Linux Foundation lists it at beginner experience level with no required prerequisites, though it recommends some hands-on exposure to AI applications and tool integrations first.

**Is the MCPA performance-based like the CKA?**

No. It is multiple choice, not a live terminal. That makes it a knowledge exam rather than a skills exam, which is worth knowing before you compare it to the CKA or CKS.

**How long is the MCPA valid?**

Two years, with a 12-month window to schedule and sit the exam after purchase, and one free retake included.

**What does the MCPA exam actually weight most?**

Interactions and execution at 26% and security and governance at 24%, so half the exam sits on the runtime behaviour and the trust model rather than on definitions. Fundamentals are 16%, architecture 14% and use cases 20%.

## Who this is for

Engineers working with PyTorch who want a vendor-neutral credential, including infrastructure people who serve models without training them.

## What it covers

- PyTorch fundamentals (38%)
- Model development (20%)
- Performance and optimization (26%)
- Data handling (16%)

*Domain names above reflect the current official curriculum's topic areas; exact weightings are set by the Linux Foundation/CNCF and revised periodically, so check their published curriculum for the current breakdown.*

## Why it's worth it

PyTorch moved to the Linux Foundation in 2022 and this is its first certification, which makes it the AI entry in a catalogue that is otherwise infrastructure. Fundamentals is 38% and performance another 26%, so it leans toward tensors, devices and making training fast rather than model architecture theory. That weighting makes it more useful to an infrastructure engineer than the title suggests.

## Prep tips

- Fundamentals is 38% and it means tensors, devices and the training loop. If you use PyTorch through a higher-level wrapper, drop down a level before sitting it.
- Performance and optimization at 26% covers precision, execution optimisation and distributed training, which is where the infrastructure overlap is. Know what moves between CPU, CUDA and MPS and what it costs.
- Data handling is only 16% but Datasets, DataLoaders and transforms are easy marks if you have ever built a pipeline.

## Frequently asked questions

**What is the PTCA certification?**

The PyTorch Certified Associate, a 120-minute multiple-choice exam covering PyTorch fundamentals, model development, performance and optimisation, and data handling. PyTorch is a Linux Foundation project.

**How much is the PTCA with a discount code?**

List price is $250. With RUSHABH30 it drops to about $175, a saving of roughly $75.

**Is PTCA useful if I do infrastructure rather than machine learning?**

More than you would expect. Fundamentals and performance are 64% between them, and both are about tensors, devices and making things run efficiently, which is closer to infrastructure work than to model research.

**Do I need a GPU to prepare?**

Not strictly. The exam covers device basics across CPU, CUDA and MPS, and you can learn the concepts on a laptop. Access to a GPU helps for the distributed-training portion of the performance domain.

# Privacy Policy

Effective July 10, 2026 · rushabhshah.dev

\# TL;DR

No ads. No creepy tracking. No cookies from me. I count page views without knowing who you are, I read the messages you send me, and that's about it. If you click a coupon link, the store's own cookies take over, not mine.

Hi. This site is just me, [Rushabh](https://rushabhshah.dev/). It's a personal website, not a business, so there isn't much to disclose. But you deserve to know exactly what happens when you visit, so here it is.

## I count visits, not visitors

I use [GoatCounter](https://www.goatcounter.com) to see which pages people read. It tells me things like "120 people read this post, mostly from India, mostly on Chrome." It can't tell me *who* those people were. There are no cookies, no stored IP addresses, no following you around the internet. Some of these numbers are shown right on the site (the little "views" counters).

## If you message me, I read it

The contact form sends me your name, email, and message (through a service called [Pageclip](https://pageclip.co)). I use it to reply to you. That's it. You won't end up on a mailing list, and I don't pass it to anyone. Prefer plain email? [contact@rushabhshah.dev](mailto:contact@rushabhshah.dev).

## The coupon links earn me a commission

My [Linux Foundation coupon page](https://rushabhshah.dev/linux-foundation-coupon/) has affiliate links. Click one and buy something, and I earn a small commission. You pay nothing extra. To make that work, the store and its affiliate network set a cookie on *their* site so they know I sent you. My site doesn't set any affiliate cookies itself, and I always label affiliate stuff clearly.

## A few files come from other servers

Fonts come from Google, icons from a couple of icon CDNs, my GitHub star counts from GitHub's API. When your browser fetches those files, those servers see your IP address, the same as they would for any website. I don't use any of it to identify you. The site itself is hosted on [GitHub Pages](https://pages.github.com), which keeps standard server logs.

## Want something deleted? Ask

The only personal data I ever hold is correspondence you sent me yourself. If you want it gone, email me at [contact@rushabhshah.dev](mailto:contact@rushabhshah.dev) and I'll delete it. No forms, no fuss. The analytics can't be traced back to you even if I wanted to, which is the point.

## If you sign up for sale alerts

Some of the coupon pages have a box to leave your email address so I can tell you when a certification sale beats my everyday partner codes. If you use it, here's exactly what happens.

**What I store:** your email address, which page you signed up from, and the time you did it. Nothing else. I don't ask for your name and I don't attach any browsing history to it.

**Where it goes:** Pageclip, the same form host the contact form on my homepage uses. It sits there until I send an alert. I don't sell it, rent it, or hand it to an advertiser, and I don't use it to build a profile of you.

**What you'll get:** a short email when a sale lands that's genuinely better than the everyday codes, which realistically means a few times a year. Not a newsletter, and not a drip sequence.

**Getting out:** reply to any alert and say so, or email [contact@rushabhshah.dev](mailto:contact@rushabhshah.dev). I'll delete the address rather than just flagging it unsubscribed, and you don't have to give a reason.

## If anything changes

If I ever add something that collects more (a newsletter signup, for example), I'll update this page first and change the date at the top. No silent changes.
